topic: Terraform: state, modules, workspaces, drift, CI
why: An FDE stands up the customer's environment on week one and hands it to their two-person platform team on week twelve; if the VPC, IAM roles and cluster were built by clicking, nobody can reproduce it in the second region, nobody can audit who changed the security group, and the hand-over is a screenshot deck. Terraform with remote state and plan-on-PR is how you turn 'trust me, it is configured' into a reviewable diff the customer's security team can sign, and how you avoid the two career-ending moments: applying dev code to their production account, and a plan that quietly says 'forces replacement' on the database. Senior FDE loops at Palantir, Anthropic and Databricks ask about state corruption, drift and blast radius because those are the incidents that actually happen at customer sites.
prerequisites: AWS vocabulary at console level: VPC, subnet, route table, internet and NAT gateway, security group, EC2, IAM role; the full depth arrives in 'AWS networking and compute: VPC, subnets, SG, NACL, ALB across AZs, EC2, Lambda' (topic 13), which you should run in parallel with this one

IAM assume-role mechanics: what a trust policy is, what `aws sts get-caller-identity` and `aws sts assume-role` return, and why a role with an OIDC trust beats an access key; deepened in 'IAM and cloud security: least privilege, roles, IRSA, no long-lived keys' (topic 15)

Shell and Git from topics 0 and 4: `jq` over JSON, exit codes in `if` and `set -e`, environment variable precedence, Git tags versus branches, protected branches and required status checks, because plan-on-PR is a Git workflow first
A sandbox AWS account with a billing alarm at 20 USD, AWS CLI v2 configured with an SSO profile or named profile, and the account ID memorised so you recognise it in `allowed_account_ids` and ARNs
Terraform 1.10 or newer installed through tfenv or mise (so `use_lockfile`, ephemeral values, import and removed blocks all exist), plus tflint, trivy, conftest and jq on PATH
Comfort reading a directed acyclic graph and a JSON document a few thousand lines long; state files and plan JSON are both

subtopics.name: init, providers, the dependency lock file, and the graph plan builds
subtopics.learn: `terraform init` resolves `required_providers` constraints (`~> 5.0` means >= 5.0, < 6.0), downloads provider binaries into `.terraform/providers/`, and writes `.terraform.lock.hcl` with `h1:` and `zh:` hashes per platform; commit the lock file, and run `terraform providers lock -platform=linux_amd64 -platform=darwin_arm64` so a lock generated on a Mac does not fail with a checksum error in Linux CI. Set `required_version` in a `terraform {}` block so a colleague on 1.5 cannot apply a config using 1.10 features. Plan builds a DAG from references (`aws_subnet.a.vpc_id` implies an edge) and explicit `depends_on`; render it with `terraform graph | dot -Tsvg > g.svg` and know the default `-parallelism=10` walks that graph concurrently. Understand 'known after apply': any attribute the provider only returns after creation is unknown at plan, and anything computed from it becomes unknown too.

subtopics.name: Reading a plan like a reviewer: symbols, forces replacement, saved plans, exit codes
subtopics.learn: Know the six change markers cold: `+` create, `-` destroy, `~` update in place, `-/+` destroy then create, `+/-` create then destroy (create_before_destroy), `<=` read data source during apply. Every `-/+` line has a `# forces replacement` comment on the attribute responsible; that comment is the single most important line in any review. Use `terraform plan -out=tfplan` then `terraform show -json tfplan | jq '[.resource_changes[] | select(.change.actions | index("delete"))] | length'` to fail CI on any destroy; a saved plan is a binary bound to the exact config, state serial and provider versions, and it contains sensitive values in plaintext. `-detailed-exitcode` returns 0 no changes, 1 error, 2 changes, which is what drift jobs key on. `-refresh=false` speeds a plan on a large state; `-target=module.network` is an emergency tool that leaves the rest of the graph unplanned and should never appear in CI; `-replace=aws_instance.bastion` is the modern `taint`.

subtopics.name: State internals: what is in terraform.tfstate and why it exists
subtopics.learn: Open a real state file: `version: 4`, `terraform_version`, `serial` (monotonic counter, bumped on every write), `lineage` (UUID assigned at creation; a mismatch means two unrelated states), and `resources[]` each with `mode` (managed or data), `type`, `name`, `module`, `provider`, and `instances[]` carrying `schema_version`, `index_key`, `attributes`, `dependencies` and `sensitive_attributes`. State is the map from Terraform address to real-world ID plus a cache of last-known attributes; without it Terraform cannot tell 'create' from 'update'. Everything a provider returns lands in `attributes` in plaintext, including `random_password.result` and RDS master passwords. Practise `terraform state pull > backup.json` before any surgery and `terraform state push -force` only for a deliberate lineage or serial override. Hand-editing state is a last resort and requires bumping `serial`.

resource.label: Terraform docs: State purpose and structure

subtopics.name: S3 remote backend: locking, encryption, partial config and the bootstrap problem
subtopics.learn: Write `backend "s3" { bucket, key = "network/prod.tfstate", region, encrypt = true, kms_key_id, use_lockfile = true }` (1.10+ native S3 conditional-write locking creating `key.tflock`) or the older `dynamodb_table` with a `LockID` string hash key; `assume_role { role_arn }` inside the backend lets state live in a separate audit account. Backend blocks cannot reference variables, so use partial configuration: `terraform init -backend-config=envs/prod.s3.tfbackend`, and know `-migrate-state` (copy local to remote) versus `-reconfigure` (forget the old backend). The chicken-and-egg: the bucket must exist before the first init, so keep a tiny `bootstrap/` root with local state that creates the bucket with versioning (your only undo for a bad push), Block Public Access, SSE-KMS and a bucket policy denying `aws:SecureTransport = false`, then either import it or accept that one root is local. IAM for the CI role: `s3:ListBucket` on the bucket, `s3:GetObject/PutObject/DeleteObject` on the state prefix, `kms:Decrypt/GenerateDataKey` on the key, and for DynamoDB `GetItem/PutItem/DeleteItem` on the lock table. 'Error acquiring the state lock' means a run is active or died; `terraform force-unlock <LOCK_ID>` only after confirming no apply is in flight.

subtopics.name: State surgery: state mv/rm/list/show, import blocks, moved and removed blocks
subtopics.learn: `terraform state list`, `terraform state show aws_vpc.main`, `terraform state mv 'module.old.aws_subnet.x[0]' 'module.net.aws_subnet.x["a"]'` (single-quote addresses so the shell leaves brackets alone), and `terraform state rm` to stop managing something without destroying it. Prefer declarative equivalents that go through code review: `moved { from = aws_instance.web  to = module.compute.aws_instance.web }` for zero-downtime refactors across module boundaries, `removed { from = aws_s3_bucket.logs  lifecycle { destroy = false } }` (1.7+), and `import { to = aws_vpc.main  id = "vpc-0abc123" }` (1.5+) combined with `terraform plan -generate-config-out=generated.tf` to write the HCL for you. Import IDs are provider-specific and documented in the Import section of every resource page: an `aws_security_group_rule` ID is a composite string, an `aws_iam_role_policy_attachment` is `role-name/policy-arn`. The exit criterion for adoption is a plan that says 'No changes' with no `-target` and no `ignore_changes` hiding real differences.

subtopics.name: Module design: structure, inputs as an API, pinned sources, no provider blocks inside
subtopics.learn: Standard layout: `main.tf`, `variables.tf`, `outputs.tf`, `versions.tf`, `README.md`, `examples/complete/`. Sources: registry `source = "terraform-aws-modules/vpc/aws"  version = "~> 5.0"`, Git `source = "git::https://github.com/org/modules.git//vpc?ref=v1.4.0"` pinned to a tag or SHA and never a branch, local `./modules/x` for the same repo. A child module declares `required_providers` but never a `provider` block; the root passes providers with `providers = { aws = aws.us_west_2 }` and the child lists `configuration_aliases` when it needs more than one. Outputs are the module's contract: export IDs, ARNs and CIDRs, not whole resource objects, because whole objects leak schema changes to every consumer. Keep modules cohesive (one network, one cluster), refuse 80-variable 'wrapper' modules, and add `validation {}` blocks and `optional()` attributes with defaults so callers get an error at plan rather than an AWS API error at apply.

subtopics.name: for_each versus count, dynamic blocks, and the index-shift trap
subtopics.learn: `count` produces list-indexed instances (`aws_subnet.private[0]`), so removing or reordering an element shifts every later index and the plan destroys and recreates them; `for_each` over a `map` or `set(string)` yields stable keys (`aws_subnet.private["eu-west-1a"]`). Build maps with `for_each = { for s in var.subnets : s.name => s }` and reference `each.key` and `each.value`. Keys must be known at plan time: `toset(aws_subnet.x[*].id)` fails with 'keys derived from resource attributes that cannot be determined until apply', so key on static names, not IDs. Convert `count` to `for_each` with one `moved` block per instance (`from = aws_subnet.private[0]  to = aws_subnet.private["a"]`) or the plan will be all destroys. `dynamic "ingress" { for_each = var.rules  content { from_port = ingress.value.port ... } }` generates nested blocks; keep `try()`, `lookup()`, `one()` and `coalesce()` in reach for optional structure.

subtopics.name: lifecycle meta-arguments and controlling replacement
subtopics.learn: `lifecycle { create_before_destroy = true }` flips `-/+` to `+/-` so a replacement never leaves a gap, but it propagates to dependents and collides with fixed `name` values, so pair it with `name_prefix`. `prevent_destroy = true` makes any plan that would destroy the resource error out, including a full `terraform destroy`, and does nothing if the resource block itself is deleted from config. `ignore_changes = [tags["LastScanned"], desired_capacity]` is the fix for attributes owned by another controller (cluster autoscaler, a Lambda deploy pipeline, a security scanner adding tags). `replace_triggered_by = [terraform_data.revision]` recreates a resource when something unrelated changes; `terraform_data` is the built-in replacement for `null_resource`. `precondition` and `postcondition` blocks turn assumptions ('the AMI is x86_64', 'the subnet has an IPv4 CIDR') into plan-time errors with a readable message.

subtopics.name: Variables, locals, outputs: precedence, type constraints, sensitive and ephemeral
subtopics.learn: Assignment precedence, lowest to highest: `TF_VAR_name` env vars, `terraform.tfvars`, `*.auto.tfvars` in lexical order, then `-var` and `-var-file` in command-line order. Write real types: `object({ cidr = string, azs = optional(list(string), []), nat = optional(bool, true) })` so callers get a type error rather than a silent default, and `validation { condition = can(cidrnetmask(var.cidr))  error_message = "cidr must be IPv4 CIDR" }`. `sensitive = true` redacts plan output and forces `sensitive = true` on any output that carries it, but the value is still in state; `ephemeral = true` (1.10+) is the flag that keeps a value out of state and plan files entirely. `terraform output -raw kubeconfig > ~/.kube/config` and `terraform output -json` are the CI-facing forms. Use `locals` for `merge(var.tags, { ManagedBy = "terraform", Env = var.env })` and provider `default_tags` so every resource is tagged without touching each block.

subtopics.name: Environment strategy: CLI workspaces versus directory-per-environment versus Terragrunt
subtopics.learn: CLI workspaces (`terraform workspace new prod`, `terraform.workspace` in expressions) store state under `env:/prod/<key>` in the same bucket with the same backend credentials and the same provider config; that means one IAM role can touch every environment and a forgotten `workspace select` applies dev values to prod. Directory-per-environment (`envs/dev`, `envs/prod`, each with its own `.s3.tfbackend`, its own `assume_role` target and `allowed_account_ids`) gives real credential and state separation at the cost of duplicated root boilerplate; Terragrunt removes that duplication with `generate` blocks and `run-all`. The FDE default for a customer with separate accounts: one state per (account, region, layer), layers split into network, data and compute so plan time stays under a few minutes and a broken compute plan cannot lock the network state; pass IDs between layers with `terraform_remote_state` or SSM parameters, never by copy-paste.

subtopics.name: Drift: refresh-only, reconciling click-ops, and the things refresh cannot see
subtopics.learn: Drift is real infrastructure differing from state. `terraform plan -refresh-only` shows exactly what changed outside Terraform without proposing config changes; `terraform apply -refresh-only` accepts reality into state. A normal plan refreshes first and then diffs config against the refreshed state, so a manual security group rule shows up as a `~` update reverting it. Schedule `plan -detailed-exitcode -lock-timeout=2m` nightly; exit 2 means drift, page or open an issue. Triage each diff into one of three actions: revert (someone opened 0.0.0.0/0 on 22), adopt (import the resource they created in the console), or ignore (`ignore_changes` for an attribute owned by an autoscaler or a deploy pipeline). Refresh only inspects addresses already in state, so resources created outside Terraform are invisible to it; that gap needs AWS Config rules or a tag-based sweep (`aws resourcegroupstaggingapi get-resources` filtered on missing `ManagedBy`). A resource deleted manually shows as `+ create`; a resource removed from state but not AWS becomes an orphan billing you forever.

subtopics.name: Plan on PR, apply on merge: the GitHub Actions pipeline
subtopics.learn: On `pull_request`: `terraform fmt -check -recursive`, `init -input=false -backend-config=...`, `validate`, tflint, trivy config, then `plan -out=tfplan -no-color -input=false -lock-timeout=5m` with `TF_IN_AUTOMATION=1` and `TF_INPUT=0`; post the plan as a PR comment (GitHub truncates at 65,536 characters, so summarise counts and attach the full plan as an artifact) and upload `tfplan` with a short retention because it contains secrets. On `push` to `main`: either apply the exact saved plan from the merged PR or re-plan and `apply -auto-approve`, inside `concurrency: { group: terraform-prod, cancel-in-progress: false }` so applies serialise, and inside a GitHub Environment with required reviewers for prod. Use `hashicorp/setup-terraform` with `terraform_wrapper: false` when you need real exit codes. The plan job executes provider code and data sources, so it must never receive apply credentials and must never run for forks with secrets (`pull_request_target` is the classic mistake). Separate plan and apply roles; the plan role needs read on AWS plus write on the state lock only.

resource.label: Terraform tutorial: Running Terraform in automation

subtopics.name: OIDC federation from GitHub Actions to AWS: no long-lived keys
subtopics.learn: Add `permissions: id-token: write` to the job and call `aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials` with `role-to-assume` and `aws-region`; the action exchanges GitHub's OIDC token for STS credentials via `AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity`. In AWS, create the `token.actions.githubusercontent.com` identity provider once, then a role whose trust policy checks `aud` = `sts.amazonaws.com` and `sub` with `StringLike` on `repo:org/repo:ref:refs/heads/main` for the apply role and `repo:org/repo:pull_request` for the plan role; a wildcard `repo:org/*` lets any repo in the org assume your prod role. Set `role-duration-seconds` to the minimum that covers your longest apply. Verify with `aws sts get-caller-identity` as the first step of every job so the account ID is in the log. This is the pattern you will be asked to reproduce at every customer that still has `AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID` in repository secrets.

resource.label: GitHub Docs: Configuring OpenID Connect in Amazon Web Services

subtopics.name: Static checks and policy: tflint, trivy/checkov, conftest on plan JSON, terraform test
subtopics.learn: `terraform validate` is schema-only and never calls AWS, so it will pass an invalid instance type; tflint with the AWS ruleset (`.tflint.hcl` with `plugin "aws" { enabled = true  version = "..."  source = "github.com/terraform-linters/tflint-ruleset-aws" }`) catches that plus deprecated syntax and unused declarations. `trivy config .` or `checkov -d .` flag misconfiguration classes: unencrypted S3, security groups open to the world on 22 or 3389, IAM wildcards. Policy on the plan is stronger than policy on the source because it sees resolved values: `terraform show -json tfplan > plan.json` then `conftest test plan.json -p policy/` with Rego rules that deny any `resource_changes[_]` where `change.actions` contains `delete` for `aws_db_instance` or where `tags.Owner` is missing. `terraform test` (1.6+) runs `.tftest.hcl` files with `run` blocks, `command = plan` and `assert` conditions so module contracts are tested without creating resources. Order in CI: fmt, validate, tflint, scanner, plan, policy, comment.

subtopics.name: Provider configuration for multi-account, multi-region: aliases, assume_role, allowed_account_ids
subtopics.learn: `provider "aws" { region = "eu-west-1"  assume_role { role_arn = var.deploy_role_arn  session_name = "terraform"  external_id = var.external_id }  default_tags { tags = local.tags }  allowed_account_ids = [var.account_id] }`. `allowed_account_ids` makes the provider refuse to run if `AWS_PROFILE` points at the wrong account, and it is the cheapest guard you will ever add against applying a sandbox config to a customer's production. A second `provider "aws" { alias = "dr"  region = "us-west-2" }` is used with `provider = aws.dr` on a resource or `providers = { aws = aws.dr }` on a module. Never put credentials in HCL; understand the credential chain the provider walks (env vars, shared config profile with SSO, ECS or EC2 instance metadata, IRSA web identity) so you can explain which identity a given plan ran as. `data "aws_caller_identity" "current"` and `data "aws_region" "current"` belong in every root so ARNs are never hard-coded.

subtopics.name: Debugging and recovery: TF_LOG, partial applies, errored.tfstate, lock and hash errors
subtopics.learn: `TF_LOG=DEBUG TF_LOG_PATH=./tf.log terraform apply` (levels TRACE, DEBUG, INFO, WARN, ERROR; `TF_LOG_CORE` and `TF_LOG_PROVIDER` split them) shows the exact AWS API call and response behind an opaque error. A failed apply is normal and partial: every resource that completed is already in state, so the recovery is to read the error, fix, and plan again, never to delete state. If Terraform cannot write state to the backend after applying, it drops `errored.tfstate` in the working directory and tells you; recover with `terraform state push errored.tfstate` before anyone else runs. 'Provider produced inconsistent final plan' is almost always a provider bug or an unknown value that changed between plan and apply; 'Cycle:' errors come from `depends_on` or mutual references and `terraform graph` shows the loop. Set resource `timeouts { create = "30m" }` for EKS and RDS, use `-parallelism=5` when the AWS API throttles, and fix 'checksum mismatch' in the lock file with `providers lock -platform=...` rather than deleting `.terraform.lock.hcl`.

subtopics.name: Building the deliverable: VPC, subnets, NAT and EC2 with the community VPC module, ready for EKS
subtopics.learn: Consume `terraform-aws-modules/vpc/aws` with `cidr`, `azs = slice(data.aws_availability_zones.available.names, 0, 3)`, `private_subnets` and `public_subnets` computed with `cidrsubnet(var.cidr, 4, i)`, `enable_nat_gateway = true`, `single_nat_gateway = true` for dev (one gateway, roughly 32 USD a month plus data) versus `one_nat_gateway_per_az = true` for prod HA, and `enable_dns_hostnames = true`. Tag subnets now so the EKS topic (16) works later: `public_subnet_tags = { "kubernetes.io/role/elb" = 1 }` and `private_subnet_tags = { "kubernetes.io/role/internal-elb" = 1 }`. Add VPC endpoints for S3 (gateway) and ECR (interface) so image pulls do not pay NAT egress. Launch EC2 from `data "aws_ami"` filtered on `al2023-ami-*` with `most_recent = true` and `owners = ["amazon"]`, an instance profile with `AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore` so there is no SSH key and no port 22, and a security group with no inbound rules. Output `vpc_id`, `private_subnet_ids`, `public_subnet_ids`. Finish every session with `terraform destroy` or a nightly destroy job in the sandbox.

subtopics.name: Secrets in state and what never to put in Terraform
subtopics.learn: State stores every returned attribute in plaintext: `random_password.db.result`, `aws_db_instance.password`, `aws_iam_access_key.secret`, `tls_private_key.private_key_pem`. Mitigate in layers: SSE-KMS on the bucket with a key policy that only the CI roles and a break-glass group can decrypt, bucket policy scoped to those principals, S3 access logging on. Remove the secret from state where the provider allows it: `manage_master_user_password = true` on `aws_db_instance` puts the password in Secrets Manager and leaves only an ARN in state; write-only arguments (1.11+, suffixed `_wo`) and ephemeral resources (1.10+) let you pass a secret at apply without persisting it. Remember `sensitive = true` hides values from CLI output only; `terraform show -json` and the plan artifact reveal them, so lock down CI logs and artifact retention. Do not template kubeconfigs or tokens into local files with `local_file`, and do not manage things that change hourly (feature flags, Lambda code) in the same state as the network.

resource.label: Terraform docs: Sensitive Data in State

outcomes: You can bootstrap an S3 remote backend with versioning, SSE-KMS and locking (use_lockfile or DynamoDB), migrate an existing local state into it with `init -migrate-state`, and name every IAM permission the CI role needs and why.

You can read any plan and, before approving, list which resources will be replaced and which attribute forces it, then rewrite the change so the plan is non-destructive using moved blocks, state mv, ignore_changes, or create_before_destroy as appropriate.

You can adopt an existing click-ops VPC, its subnets and security groups into a module using import blocks and -generate-config-out, and end with `terraform plan` reporting 'No changes' without -target or hidden ignore_changes.

You can write a module with typed object inputs using optional() defaults and validation blocks, no provider block inside, a pinned Git or registry source, and consume it from two environment roots with separate backends, assume_role targets and allowed_account_ids.

You can build a GitHub Actions pipeline that plans on PR under a read-only OIDC role, posts the plan and uploads the artifact, and applies on merge under a separate role inside a concurrency group and a protected environment, with zero AWS access keys anywhere.
You can run a drift review: execute plan -refresh-only, classify every diff as revert, adopt or ignore with a one-line justification, and explain why resources created outside Terraform never appear.

You can recover from a stale lock (force-unlock with a verified lock ID), an errored.tfstate after a backend write failure, and a lock-file checksum mismatch between macOS and Linux CI, each in under ten minutes.

You can argue for an environment isolation strategy (workspaces, directories, Terragrunt) for a customer with three AWS accounts in terms of blast radius, credential separation and plan time, and state what would make you change it.
failureModes: A subnet list built with count gets a new AZ inserted at position 1; the plan replaces two subnets, the apply destroys the ones the customer's RDS subnet group depends on, RDS refuses the change, and state is left half-applied on a Friday evening.

Two engineers apply from laptops against the same S3 backend configured without locking; the second write overwrites the first's state, and the next plan proposes creating 40 resources that already exist, each failing with AlreadyExists.
A workflow uses pull_request_target so plan runs on forks with the apply role; a contributor's PR adds an `external` data source that curls the OIDC token and STS credentials to their server.

The RDS master password and an IAM user's secret key sit in plaintext in state, the state bucket grants s3:GetObject to an engineering-wide role, and the customer's SOC 2 auditor lists it as a finding against your delivery.

A module source pins `ref=main` instead of a tag; a colleague pushes an unrelated change, and the next prod PR's plan shows a NAT gateway replacement nobody asked for, approved by a reviewer who only read the PR description.
Nobody set ignore_changes on the EKS managed node group scaling_config.desired_size; every apply after the cluster autoscaler scales up resets the node count to 2 and evicts customer workloads.

An engineer with AWS_PROFILE pointing at the customer's production account applies the sandbox root because the code is identical and allowed_account_ids was never set; the plan output scrolled past and the prod NAT gateway is gone.
interviewQuestions: Walk me through exactly what happens between `terraform plan` and `terraform apply`: what the lock protects against, what 'known after apply' means, why a plan can succeed and the apply fail, and what state looks like after a failed apply.

A customer has a hand-built VPC with six subnets, twelve security groups and an ALB and wants it under Terraform with zero downtime. Design the adoption: how you import, how you prove the plan is clean, what you do about resources whose config cannot be made to match, and what the first production PR contains.

Your PR plan shows `-/+ aws_db_instance.main (forces replacement)` because someone renamed the identifier. The customer cannot take downtime. Give me your options in order of preference and what each does to state.

Design Terraform CI/CD across dev, staging and prod in three AWS accounts. Where do credentials come from, how do you stop a fork PR from exfiltrating them, how do you stop two applies racing on the same state, and where exactly does a human approve?

A nightly drift job started returning exit code 2 every night on an aws_autoscaling_group and nobody changed anything. What is happening, what are three ways to fix it, and which would you choose for a customer whose platform team will own this in six months?

Workspaces versus directory-per-environment versus Terragrunt: pick one for a customer deployment you will hand over, defend it in terms of blast radius and credentials, and tell me what would make you change your mind.

An engineer ran `terraform state push` with a week-old file and now the plan wants to create everything. What do you do in the first fifteen minutes, and what structural change stops it from happening again?
proofOfWork: A public repository, tf-aws-foundation, laid out as modules/network and modules/compute plus envs/dev and envs/prod roots, each root with its own .s3.tfbackend, assume_role target and allowed_account_ids, and a bootstrap/ root that creates the versioned SSE-KMS state bucket and OIDC provider. GitHub Actions plan on PR under a read-only role and apply on merge under a separate role behind a protected environment and a concurrency group; conftest policies that deny untagged resources and any delete on aws_db_instance or aws_s3_bucket; tflint and trivy in the same pipeline. A recorded terminal session (asciinema or pasted output in the README) demonstrates three things end to end: (1) a VPC created by hand with the AWS CLI is adopted with import blocks and -generate-config-out until plan says No changes; (2) a count-based subnet set is migrated to for_each with moved blocks and the plan shows zero destroys; (3) a security group rule added in the console is caught by the nightly plan -detailed-exitcode job and reverted by the next apply. A one-page ADR in the repo explains the choice of directory-per-environment over workspaces and the network/data/compute state layering, in language a customer platform lead could sign off on.
